encounters.cc: Follow-up visit one month after initiation of lisinopril for severe hypertension, now with acute kidney injury

lines: Follow-up visit one month after initiation of lisinopril for severe hypertension, now with acute kidney injury
One month ago, his blood pressure was 196/114 mm Hg during an annual physical, and he was started on lisinopril.
At that time, his serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, and serum electrolytes were normal.
Today, he feels well and has no complaints.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
- Multiple episodes of nephrolithiasis managed conservatively
- Insulin glargine 24 units subcutaneous at bedtime
- Father: Myocardial infarction at age 62, hypertension
- One brother with history of kidney stones
He does not use NSAIDs or herbal supplements.
His blood pressure is 172/92 mm Hg.
Physical examination shows no bruits, edema, or rash.
Repeat labs reveal a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL and no proteinuria or hematuria.

encounters.cc: Difficult-to-control blood pressure despite triple therapy with rising creatinine

lines: Difficult-to-control blood pressure despite triple therapy with rising creatinine
This 55-year-old male with severe hypertension and CKD Stage 3a returns three months after his Internal Medicine visit with acute kidney injury after lisinopril initiation.
Despite adherence to hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, and metoprolol, his blood pressure remains elevated at 162/98 mmHg.
He reports no symptoms of headache, vision changes, or chest pain.
Laboratory tests show a serum creatinine increase from 1.0 mg/dL to 1.4 mg/dL since that visit when lisinopril was started.
- Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
- Multiple episodes of nephrolithiasis managed conservatively
His current medications include lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, amlodipine, metoprolol, and atorvastatin.

lines: Bilateral breast tenderness and enlargement two months after starting spironolactone
The patient with severe hypertension complicated by renal artery stenosis and prior medication-induced AKI returns with breast symptoms following recent medication adjustment.
Two months ago, his cardiologist started him on an additional medication to improve blood pressure control and reduce symptoms of fluid overload.
Since then, he has developed breast tenderness and enlargement that is causing him embarrassment.
He denies nipple discharge, skin changes, or pain elsewhere.

encounters.cc: Severe left flank pain radiating to groin with nausea and urinary frequency

lines: Severe left flank pain radiating to groin with nausea and urinary frequency
This 57-year-old male with recurrent nephrolithiasis and CKD Stage 3a, most recently seen in November 2021 for hypokalemia, presents with flank pain.
The pain is constant, radiates to the groin, and is associated with nausea.
He reports a recent increase in the frequency of urination, often feeling that he cannot completely empty his bladder.
He also mentions having had a few episodes of nocturia with large urine volumes.
- Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis (diagnosed 2020-04-15)

encounters.cc: Fever, increasing abdominal girth, and acute confusion in patient with known cirrhosis

lines: Fever, increasing abdominal girth, and acute confusion in patient with known cirrhosis
The patient with known alcohol-related cirrhosis and recurrent nephrolithiasis returns with recurrent abdominal distension, having presented similarly in November 2021.
He presents to the emergency department with a two-day history of increasing abdominal girth and discomfort.
He also reports feeling feverish and has experienced a recent onset of confusion.
His wife notes that he has been less responsive and has not been eating well.

lines: Severe scrotal and perineal pain with swelling, fever, and chills

This 58-year-old male with alcohol-related cirrhosis, severe hypertension, and prior spontaneous bacterial peritonitis six months ago presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of severe pain and swelling in the scrotal and perineal area.
He reports a high fever and chills that started suddenly the previous night.

lines: Worsening diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and obstipation for 18 hours
This 58-year-old male with cirrhosis and prior SBP reports progressive bloating, minimal oral intake, and no passage of gas or stool since last night.
- Secondary hypertension due to renal artery stenosis (diagnosed 2020-04-15)

He denies fever, hematemesis, melena, chest pain, or urinary symptoms.
Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), blood pressure 102/66 mm Hg, pulse 112/min, and respirations 20/min
On arrival he appears uncomfortable and mildly dehydrated.
The abdomen is distended and tympanic with diffuse mild tenderness; high-pitched rushes are heard intermittently followed by quiet intervals.
No groin or incisional bulges are palpable, and rectal exam shows an empty vault.
A plain upright abdominal film is obtained.
Imaging shows multiple stacked air–fluid levels in centrally located dilated loops with little distal gas.
